doc.title: Michael Max Fleming interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 8, 2017

title: The bass player's role and keeping time in a rhythm section
summary: Fleming says the bass is the base of the harmony and that time is a consensus of the rhythm section, not one player's job. He gives his students no list of rhythm sections to study.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: My name is Monk Rowe and I’m very pleased to have bassist Michael Max Fleming with me today in preparation for a gig at Hamilton College. I’m going to start out with a real easy question: What is your idea of the role of a bass player in a band?
Well in a sense the B-A-S-S is the B-A-S-E of the harmony. Is that good enough?
That’s good. Who’s the main timekeeper in the band? Because I’ve had drummers say, “Well it’s me of course.” And then I’ve had bass players say, “It’s really me.”

Well you say main, well let me try. What it turns out to be, the predominant utterance of the rhythm section. In other words, it’s not either or. I mean some people play like that but to me that’s an inferior approach. I don’t think that way. I got the time, you got the time, although there have been times when I’ve had to dominate or people have tried to dominate me. But to me it’s about a consensus. And to me those that are successful rhythm sections are those that have the same thing in mind in working together and can feel each other. Not, “I got it, you follow me,” or “you got it.” To me that is totally beneath me in anybody I ever want to play with.
Do you have particular rhythm sections that you over the years have told your students to listen carefully to?
No. I just haven’t. Maybe I should have but I never did it.
That’s not part of my approach. That’s not part of my method.
